title: Feeding by Tourists Puts Japan's Rabbit Island at Risk
paragraphs: Okunoshima, a small island in the Seto Inland Sea near Hiroshima, is famous around the world as "Rabbit Island." Every year, large numbers of tourists take a ferry to the island to see and feed the hundreds of friendly rabbits that live there. However, researchers now warn that all this feeding may be causing serious problems for the island's environment.

The rabbits are not native to Japan, and they are believed to have been released on the island by people. According to a newspaper report from 1972, eight pairs of rabbits were released, and they had grown to more than 200. Today, there are more than 500 rabbits on the island, and they are so tame that they often run up to visitors expecting food.

Researchers from Fukushima University and the National Institute of Technology's Kure College have studied the effects of tourism on the island, and their findings were published in the Journal of Ecotourism. According to the study, the number of visitors more than doubled between 2008 and 2015. As a result, the amount of food brought by tourists rose from about 8 tons in 2013 to around 27 tons a year by 2017. The researchers believe the rabbit population is largely supported by this food.

Moreover, the feeding appears to be affecting other animals. Wild boars, which have been confirmed to breed on the island, eat leftover food, and on a small number of occasions, they have even been observed killing live rabbits. Professor Shingo Kaneko, who led the research, said that food left by tourists "may be attracting wild boars into the areas heavily populated by rabbits." Crows and black kites have also been seen eating leftover food. In addition, the rabbits have stripped the lower branches of many plants, leaving a visible line known as the "rabbit line."

However, the researchers do not recommend ending tourism or feeding. Instead, they suggest managing the amount of food and monitoring the island's wildlife. Meanwhile, authorities are asking visitors to watch the rabbits eat and take any leftover food home, warning that feeding could otherwise be banned altogether.
